# Ref Commons Playbook

When I see the sustainable share per boat, I divide the current stock by three times that share to estimate the number of boats.

When I'm deciding my catch in early seasons, I take moderately above the sustainable share—around 1.8x to 2x it—to hedge against other boats defecting while not guaranteeing collapse myself.

When the stock recovers fully after a season where catches were mixed, I recognize this as evidence that moderate overfishing by me personally hasn't been catastrophic, and I increase my catch accordingly in the next season.

When I'm in the middle seasons and have already accumulated a significant total above the fair share, I continue taking above-sustainable amounts rather than pivoting to restraint, since the other boats don't appear to be retaliating and I've already signaled my strategy.

When I reach the final season, I take as much as the stock allows without keeping anything back for future recovery, since there are no consequences beyond this round.

When I'm uncertain about the exact sustainable level, I use the stated sustainable share as a reference point and take 1.5x to 2x that amount as a working target.

**What didn't work:** In middle and late seasons, I justified moderate catches (15-18) by claiming I was "balancing" or being "reasonable," but this was rationalization—I was actually taking well above fair share and would have done better to either fully cooperate early or push harder consistently. Pick a strategy and commit to it rather than drift between greedy and moderate.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I recognize it as the cooperative equilibrium—what should happen if all boats behave rationally. I will use it as my baseline target, not as a ceiling.

When I'm deciding my catch early in the game, I will commit to taking the sustainable share each season. This locks in a predictable score and avoids the temptation to defect that grows stronger as I watch others' behavior.

When I observe another boat catching significantly more than the sustainable share, I will not use that as justification to increase my own catch. Their overfishing doesn't change the optimal strategy for me—it only signals that the stock will decline faster. I should either maintain discipline or accept that the game is already degrading.

When the stock declines noticeably below 100, I will not rationalize taking more to "get mine" before collapse. I will instead hold steady at the sustainable share. Restraint at that point is what actually saves the fishery.

When I reach the final season, I face a genuine temptation to defect and maximize my immediate score at the expense of the resource. I know this worked in my last play. But I should recognize that final-season defection is a trap: it yields only modest additional gain (I ended with 67.9, not much better than sustainable play would have) and demonstrates that I cannot be trusted as a cooperative partner. For future games where reputation or repeated play matters, I should take the sustainable share even on the last season.

When calculating what I've caught "so far," I need to remember this resets each season in terms of the sustainable share—my cumulative total matters for scoring, but each season's decision should be made fresh against that season's stock.

I will not second-guess the sustainable share with elaborate reasoning about what others might do. The math is sound. I will simply take it, season after season, and trust the system.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the initial setup, I calculate the cooperative outcome (sustainable share × number of seasons) and recognize that defection by any player collapses the resource before I can benefit from my greed.

When I'm tempted to fish beyond the sustainable share early on, I remember that I scored 71.9 when I should have scored closer to 66 with pure cooperation—my aggressive deviations cost me more than they gained me.

When I observe another boat taking significantly more than its fair share, I do not immediately retaliate by taking more myself. Matching their aggression accelerates the collapse that hurts everyone, including me. Instead, I hold to the sustainable level and let them bear the consequence of resource depletion.

When I fall behind competitively mid-game and feel the urge to catch up, I resist. Competitive desperation is how I end up taking 13 when sustainable is 10, then 27.5 in the final season, burning through a stock that was already damaged. I catch myself doing this and stick to the sustainable share.

When I reach the final season, I do not treat it as a free-for-all. Yes, there's no future to conserve for, but by that point the stock is already depleted from my earlier aggression. My final catch of 27.5 on a stock of 77.5 was justified by scarcity, not by sound strategy. I should have fished more conservatively throughout to leave more stock available at the end.

When I'm at any decision point, I ask: what total score do I end with if I stay cooperative throughout? Then I ask: how much do I actually gain by deviating now? The answer is almost always: very little, and only at the cost of future opportunity.

I fish at or slightly below the sustainable share every season except the last, where I take what remains without guilt but without recklessness either.
